- **When not to:** Let intrinsic ratio determine the box when the media is not constrained by a fixed layout slot.
- **Pitfall:** A conflicting CSS ratio can reserve one shape before load and display another after load.
- **Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-03-20 (web-features `aspect-ratio`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 89 / Safari 15.
- **See also:** [MDN: CSS aspect-ratio](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/aspect-ratio)

### L8. Stable scrollbar space

- **Rule:** Apply `scrollbar-gutter: stable` to the element that owns scrolling when content changes would shift its inline layout.
- **Why:** The stable gutter reserves space for a classic scrollbar before overflow appears.
- **When not to:** Skip it when the platform uses overlay scrollbars and reserving space would add unwanted width.
- **Pitfall:** `stable both-edges` reserves space on both sides and can make a narrow pane needlessly smaller. Without a stable gutter, a classic scrollbar can shift the inline layout.
- **Support:** Baseline newly available since 2024-12-11 (web-features `scrollbar-gutter`). Chrome 94 / Firefox 97 / Safari 18.2.
- **See also:** [MDN: CSS scrollbar-gutter](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/scrollbar-gutter)

### L9. Scroll chaining and snap points

- **Rule:** Use `overscroll-behavior: contain` on an inner pane that must stop scroll chaining, and use scroll snap only when a destination should settle at defined positions.
- **Why:** The contain value keeps overscroll from propagating to an ancestor. Scroll snap adjusts the final scroll position toward configured snap areas.
- **When not to:** Keep normal chaining when users should continue scrolling the page after reaching the end of a pane.
- **Pitfall:** The `chain` value is unavailable in some browsers. Feature-detect it and keep the default or `contain` path.
- **Support:** Baseline limited availability (web-features `overscroll-behavior`). Chrome 144 / Firefox 150 / Safari unsupported. Baseline limited availability (web-features `overscroll-behavior`). Chrome 144 / Firefox 150 / Safari unsupported. Baseline widely available since 2022-07-15 (web-features `scroll-snap`). Chrome 69 / Firefox 68 / Safari 11.
- **See also:** [MDN: CSS overscroll-behavior](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/overscroll-behavior)

### L10. Small, large and dynamic viewport heights

- **Rule:** Choose `svh` for the small visible viewport, `lvh` for the largest viewport and `dvh` when the layout should track browser chrome changes.
- **Why:** Mobile browser controls make the visible viewport change. The legacy `vh` behavior corresponds to the large viewport and can extend behind visible browser chrome.
- **When not to:** Use a content-driven height when the section should grow with its contents rather than fill a viewport.
- **Pitfall:** A `dvh` panel can resize while scrolling, while `lvh` can extend beyond the currently visible area.
- **Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
- **See also:** [MDN: Viewport-percentage length units](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/length#relative_length_units_based_on_viewport)

---

## 5. INTRINSIC SIZE ENHANCEMENTS

### L11. Content-sized controls and intrinsic-size animation

- **Rule:** Feature-detect `field-sizing: content` as an enhancement, and feature-detect `interpolate-size` or `calc-size()` as optional animation enhancements.

- **When not to:** Use a stable row count when a control must keep a fixed editing area, or omit the animation when an instant state change is clear.
- **Pitfall:** Shipping either feature as the only layout or interaction path leaves browsers without it with a fixed default size or no transition.

Chrome 129 / Firefox unsupported / Safari unsupported. Baseline limited availability (web-features `calc-size`). Chrome 129 / Firefox unsupported / Safari unsupported.
- **See also:** [MDN: CSS field-sizing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/field-sizing)

For right-to-left direction and writing-mode mapping, follow [I4 in web-internationalization.md](web-internationalization.md#i4-logical-properties-and-writing-modes).

OVERVIEW ### Purpose It covers Core Web Vitals, image and font loading, layout stability and main-thread scheduling. ### When to Use - Improving the largest contentful paint of an image. - Reserving layout space or matching font metrics to reduce layout shift. - Reducing interaction latency or rendering work for offscreen content. - Choosing responsive image sources, formats and loading hints. ### Boundaries - **Baseline media rules.** The baseline media rules remain in [web-markup-and-css.md](web-markup-and-css.md). --- ## 2. FIELD METRICS AND LCP ### P1. Largest contentful paint resource - **Rule:** Keep the likely LCP image eager, give that one image `fetchpriority="high"` and preload it when the initial markup cannot expose it early. - **Why:** The LCP target is at most 2.5 seconds at the 75th percentile. TTFB helps diagnose server delay, while preload and priority address resource discovery and scheduling in the browser. - **When not to:** Do not preload an image that is already discovered early or is not likely to become LCP. - **Pitfall:** Marking several images high priority dilutes the signal, and lazy-loading the LCP image delays its request. - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate. - **See also:** [web.dev: Optimize LCP](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp) --- ## 3. LAYOUT STABILITY AND FONTS ### P2. Cumulative layout shift - **Rule:** Reserve the final box for images, embeds and asynchronous content before their dimensions are known. - **Why:** The CLS target is at most 0.1 at the 75th percentile. A reserved box lets later content keep its position when a resource arrives. - **When not to:** Skip a reserved box when the content is already in the initial layout and has a stable intrinsic size. - **Pitfall:** Inserting a banner above existing content shifts every item below it even when the banner itself is small. Follow the web layer's [media sizing rule](web-markup-and-css.md#6-media). - **Support:** Judgment, no version gate. - **See also:** [web.dev: Optimize CLS](https://web.dev/articles/optimize-cls) ### P3. Font metrics and display strategy - **Rule:** Start with a metric-matched fallback and `size-adjust`, then use ascent, descent and line-gap overrides only as a feature-detected enhancement. - **Why:** Matching fallback glyph widths reduces line reflow before the web font loads. The override trio changes line-box metrics more directly, while `font-display: optional` favors avoiding late swaps and `swap` favors immediate text visibility. - **When not to:** Use `swap` when showing the intended face matters more than avoiding a late metric change. - **Pitfall:** Preloading a below-the-fold font can compete with the LCP resource. - **Support:** Baseline: no web-features entry. Chrome 92 / Firefox 92 / Safari 17. Baseline limited availability (web-features `font-metric-overrides`). Chrome 87 / Firefox 89 / Safari unsupported. - **See also:** [MDN: CSS @font-face](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@font-face) --- ## 4. INTERACTION AND OFFSCREEN CONTENT ### P4. Interaction to next paint - **Rule:** Break long handlers into work-sized chunks and feature-detect `scheduler.yield()` before using it to return control to the browser. Keep chunking or a worker as the baseline path. - **Why:** The INP target is at most 200 milliseconds at the 75th percentile. Yielding gives the browser a chance to process pending input and rendering before the handler continues. - **When not to:** Keep a short synchronous handler together when it completes within the interaction budget. - **Pitfall:** Yielding only after a long uninterrupted loop does not give input an earlier chance to run. - **Support:** Baseline limited availability (web-features `scheduler`). Chrome 129 / Firefox 142 / Safari unsupported. - **See also:** [MDN: Scheduler.yield()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Scheduler/yield) ### P5. Offscreen rendering with content visibility - **Rule:** Apply `content-visibility: auto` to long offscreen sections and pair it with a realistic `contain-intrinsic-size`. - **Why:** The browser can skip rendering work outside the viewport while the intrinsic size preserves a placeholder in layout. - **When not to:** Avoid it on short pages or content whose immediate layout must be measured before it approaches the viewport. - **Pitfall:** Without a placeholder size, the scrollbar can jump as skipped sections are rendered and measured.     +**Rule:** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
    +**Why:** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
    +**When not to:** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
    +**Pitfall:** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
    +**Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
    +**Rule:** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
    +**Why:** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks c
    +**When not to:** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
    +**Pitfall:** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
    +**Rule:** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
    +**Why:** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A comp
    +**When not to:** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.
    +**Pitfall:** A selector such as `.card[data-scope]` has specificity `0-2-0`, not `0-1-0`.
    +**Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
    +**Rule:** Wrap low-priority defaults in `:where()` and use `:is()` when the matching alternatives should share the strongest argument's specificity.
    +**Why:** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.
    +**When not to:** Keep a direct class selector when the alternatives would obscure which component states match.
    +**Pitfall:** Adding a high-specificity selector to one `:is()` alternative raises the specificity of the entire selector.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `is`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14. Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (we
    +**Rule:** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.
    +**Why:** The browser reevaluates relational matches as the relevant DOM changes, and a broad ancestor selector can increase style invalidation work.
    +**When not to:** Prefer an existing direct selector when the relationship is already represented by a simple parent or sibling structure.
    +**Pitfall:** A broad rule such as `body:has(.is-open)` makes unrelated subtree changes relevant to a page-level selector.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-19 (web-features `has`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 121 / Safari 15.4.

    +**When not to:** Keep a selector flat when nesting would hide its reach or increase selector complexity.

    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-11 (web-features `nesting`). Chrome 120 / Firefox 117 / Safari 17.2.
    +**Rule:** Use `@scope` to limit a rule to a component subtree when the required browsers support it.
    +**Why:** Scoped rules stop at the declared scope boundary, and scope proximity breaks a tie after specificity without changing the selector's specificity.
    +**When not to:** Use the established component scoping mechanism when a target browser does not support `@scope`.

    +**Support:** Baseline newly available since 2026-03-24 (web-features `scope`). Chrome 143 / Firefox 146 / Safari 26.4.

    +**Why:** Registration gives the browser a syntax, an `inherits` setting and an initial value, which lets typed values interpolate during animation.

    +**Rule:** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.
    +**Why:** The cascade compares these criteria in order, so a later rule cannot win by source order when an earlier criterion already decided the result.
    +**When not to:** Skip the comparison when the declarations do not apply to the same element and property.
    +**Pitfall:** Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers, while important declarations reverse layer precedence.
    +**Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
    +**Rule:** Declare the cascade layer order once in a global stylesheet before component styles load.
    +**Why:** Layer order is established the first time each layer name appears. Component style injection can vary with load order, so per-component layer blocks c
    +**When not to:** Use unlayered styles only when the app deliberately relies on the unlayered precedence boundary.
    +**Pitfall:** A deeply scoped rule inside a layer loses to an unlayered rule even when its selector looks stronger.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2024-09-14 (web-features `cascade-layers`). Chrome 99 / Firefox 97 / Safari 15.4.
    +**Rule:** Count IDs, class-like selectors and type selectors in separate specificity columns before changing a selector.
    +**Why:** IDs add to the first column, classes, attributes and pseudo-classes add to the second, and type selectors and pseudo-elements add to the third. A comp
    +**When not to:** Do not raise specificity when the actual conflict comes from origin, importance or cascade layer order.
    +**Pitfall:** A selector such as `.card[data-scope]` has specificity `0-2-0`, not `0-1-0`.
    +**Support:** Judgment, no version gate.
    +**Rule:** Wrap low-priority defaults in `:where()` and use `:is()` when the matching alternatives should share the strongest argument's specificity.
    +**Why:** `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` contributes the specificity of its most specific argument.
    +**When not to:** Keep a direct class selector when the alternatives would obscure which component states match.
    +**Pitfall:** Adding a high-specificity selector to one `:is()` alternative raises the specificity of the entire selector.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (web-features `is`). Chrome 88 / Firefox 82 / Safari 14. Baseline widely available since 2023-07-21 (we
    +**Rule:** Keep `:has()` selectors narrow and close to the component that owns the matching relationship.
    +**Why:** The browser reevaluates relational matches as the relevant DOM changes, and a broad ancestor selector can increase style invalidation work.
    +**When not to:** Prefer an existing direct selector when the relationship is already represented by a simple parent or sibling structure.
    +**Pitfall:** A broad rule such as `body:has(.is-open)` makes unrelated subtree changes relevant to a page-level selector.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-19 (web-features `has`). Chrome 105 / Firefox 121 / Safari 15.4.
    +**Rule:** Use `&` to make the parent selector explicit inside native CSS nesting.
    +**Why:** The nesting selector represents the full parent selector, so `&:hover` and `.theme &` express relationships without Sass-style string concatenation.
    +**When not to:** Keep a selector flat when nesting would hide its reach or increase selector complexity.
    +**Pitfall:** `&-active` does not append a suffix to a class name as it would in Sass.
    +**Support:** Baseline widely available since 2026-06-11 (web-features `nesting`). Chrome 120 / Firefox 117 / Safari 17.2.
    +**Rule:** Use `@scope` to limit a rule to a component subtree when the required browsers support it.
    +**Why:** Scoped rules stop at the declared scope boundary, and scope proximity breaks a tie after specificity without changing the selector's specificity.
    +**When not to:** Use the established component scoping mechanism when a target browser does not support `@scope`.
    +**Pitfall:** A scope boundary does not prevent unscoped rules from matching the same descendants. In Safari 26.0 through 26.3, rules inside `@scope` do not app
    +**Support:** Baseline newly available since 2026-03-24 (web-features `scope`). Chrome 143 / Firefox 146 / Safari 26.4.
    +**Rule:** Register a custom property with `@property` when its type, inheritance behavior or animation behavior must be explicit.
    +**Why:** Registration gives the browser a syntax, an `inherits` setting and an initial value, which lets typed values interpolate during animation.
    +**When not to:** Keep an unregistered property when it only carries an inherited token and needs no typed animation.
    +**Pitfall:** A registered property with the wrong `inherits` value can stop a theme token from reaching its descendants.
    +**Support:** Baseline newly available since 2024-07-09 (web-features `registered-custom-properties`). Chrome 85 / Firefox 128 / Safari 16.4.
    +**Rule:** Follow the state selector contract in [web-markup-and-css.md Section 7](web-markup-and-css.md#7-css-architecture).
    +**Why:** The web layer already owns how exposed state reaches CSS selectors, so this file does not define a second state source. See [A5](web-accessibility-pat
    +**When not to:** Use a class for a visual-only state that has no semantic state in the markup.
    +**Pitfall:** A store-owned `.is-open` class can drift from the expanded state already present on the control.
    +**Support:** Judgment, no version gate.

### CS1. Cascade decision order

**Rule.** Resolve competing declarations by origin and importance, layer order, specificity, scope proximity when scoped rules apply, then source order.

38: # Rule: Communication
39: 
40: > Routed from [`REPO RULES.md`](../../REPO%20RULES.md). Load before writing any substantive reply.
41: > Expands `AGENTS.md`, never overrides it. Where they appear to disagree, `AGENTS.md` wins and this file is wrong. Say so.
42: 
43: ## Fires when
44: 
45: - About to write any substantive reply, an answer, an explanation, a close-out, a status.
46: - The reader says they did not follow or asks for a plainer version.
47: 
48: ## The rule
49: 
50: **Write so the reader can act after one pass: the answer first, and nothing in the reply
51: that does not carry information.**
52: 
53: Decision shape lives in [`communication-decisions.md`](communication-decisions.md), sentence,
54: word and punctuation mechanics in [`communication-prose.md`](communication-prose.md).
55: 
56: ---
57: 
58: ## 1. THE REGISTER YOU ARE IN
59: 
60: **While working: clipped.** Act rather than narrate. Open with the result, not with
61: "I'll now" or "Let me". Batch the tool calls and report at checkpoints.
62: 
63: **At a boundary: dense.** You are at a boundary whenever the reader is about to decide
64: something, act on something or take the work over: a handoff, a close-out, a decision
65: point. Verdict first, then the receipts. Reason about the problem, not about yourself.
66: Everything else is working.
67: 
68: **Complex topic, simple words.** When the subject is technical or layered, explain it plainly the first time, not only after the reader asks: what it is, why it matters to them, what they do next. Use a term only when the reader needs it, and define it on first use. Simpler words, same claim: never drop a caveat or a number to get there.
69: 
70: The failure this prevents: the wrong register. Narration nobody reads, the verdict buried
71: in working notes or the working notes inflated into a report.
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 2. LENGTH
76: 
77: **Match length to the question.** Length is earned by the reader's need, never by the work you did to get there.
78: Every cut this file asks for has a floor, see [`communication-prose.md`](communication-prose.md) §4.
79: 
80: **Choose by reader impact before you write.** Keep what the reader would notice, act on or
81: decide differently because of. Merge the items that have the same effect for them. How the
82: work was done stays out unless it changes how far the reader can trust the result.
83: 
84: The failure this prevents: the answer is in there, and they did not find it, under a
85: record of the work they never needed.
86: 
87: **No tables in a reply,** except the in-flight block in
88: [`communication-handoff.md`](communication-handoff.md) §6. Use a sentence for one or two
89: facts and bullets for parallel items.
90: 
91: The failure this prevents: the reader parses a grid to learn what one sentence would
92: have said.
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 3. CUT FILLER
97: 
98: Every sentence carries information. The recurring offenders:

26: # Rule: Communication prose
27: 
28: > Routed from [`REPO RULES.md`](../../REPO%20RULES.md). Load before writing any substantive reply.
29: > Expands `AGENTS.md`, never overrides it. Where they appear to disagree, `AGENTS.md` wins and this file is wrong. Say so.
30: 
31: ## Fires when
32: 
33: - Drafting or editing a sentence a reader will read.
34: - Choosing between a plain and an exact word.
35: - Placing a dash, colon or semicolon.
36: - Splitting or joining sentences.
37: - Writing a paragraph.
38: 
39: ## The rule
40: 
41: **A sentence carries one idea, a paragraph stands alone, the words are plain and the
42: punctuation never trips the reader.**
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 1. SENTENCES AND PARAGRAPHS
47: 
48: **One idea per sentence.** Short, declarative, subject-verb-object where that reads
49: naturally. When a sentence stacks clauses, split it.
50: 
51: **Atomic paragraphs.** Each chunk stands alone. A reader who lands mid-reply should be
52: able to act on the paragraph in front of them without reconstructing the four above it.
53: 
54: **Vary the rhythm** of sentence length and structure. Prefer prose when a list would
55: fragment a single argument.
56: 
57: The failure this prevents: a technically correct reply the reader has to parse twice.
58: 
59: **State the relation between sentences.** Each sentence opens by saying how it attaches
60: to the one before: because, but, therefore, for example.
61: 
62: The failure this prevents: juxtaposition fakes a logical link the writer never stated,
63: and the reader supplies their own, and supplies a different one.
64: 
65: **Name the mechanism.** When a sentence explains how something works, it names the
66: moving parts: what acts, what it acts on, what changes.
67: 
68: The failure this prevents: a model whose moving parts are never named, so the reader
69: can remember it and cannot check it.
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 2. WORDS
74: 
75: Plain words by default. Reserve exact names for the things that have them, languages,
76: frameworks, APIs, dependencies, commands.
77: 
78: Introduce unavoidable jargon one term at a time, in a sentence that defines it by use.
79: 
80: The failure this prevents: the reader stops reading and starts decoding, and stops
81: noticing whether they agree.
82: 
83: Do not ship replies in terse machine register. Replace arrows or symbols standing in for
84: verbs with action words. For stacked noun phrases, say who does what, using the
85: [HVR nominalization guidance](../skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md#nominalization-and-stacked-compression).
86: Explain each ID, abbreviation or status code in plain words. Say what each bare count
87: or label measures and what it means. Turn sentence fragments into complete sentences
88: with a subject and verb, and join two of them with a full stop or a conjunction, never a
89: semicolon. The failure this prevents: readers have to guess at the action,
90: referent or result.
91: 
92: **Name an identifier only where the reader acts on it.** A path, hash, flag or ID earns its
93: place when the reader will run, open or check it. Elsewhere, say what the thing is in plain
94: words.
95: 
96: **One or two numbers to a sentence.** When the numbers are the point, give each its own
97: sentence or bullet.
98: 
99: The failure this prevents: a reply dense with names and figures the reader cannot use,
100: which buries the few they need.
101: 
102: ---
103: 
104: ## 3. PUNCTUATION THE READER TRIPS ON
105: 
106: **Never use an em dash.** Replace it with a comma, a full stop or a colon, whichever the
107: sentence actually wanted.
108: 
109: - **No semicolon.** Two sentences, or a conjunction.
110: - **No serial comma.** Drop it before the `and` or `or` that closes a list.
111: 
112: **The failure this prevents:** dashes read as authored voice to a human and as a tell to a
113: reader who has seen a lot of generated text.
114: 
115: The full standard is the Human Voice Rules, which `sk-doc` routes to. Load all of it when writing a document.
116: 
117: **In a reply, take its voice half and leave its document half.** The voice directives, the
118: vocabulary lists and the tell lists apply to anything a reader reads. The document-structure
119: sections do not. A message that presents the result of a long run is a reply by delivery and
120: a document by content, and it takes the voice half like any other reply.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 4. CONCISE IS NOT COMPRESSED
125: 
126: Concise cuts what the reader does not need and stops.
127: Compressed cuts further and takes the connective tissue with it: the because, the second
128: half of a contrast, the noun that a later "this" points back to. After a cut, check the
129: joints. If a sentence now opens on a "this" that the previous sentence no longer feeds,
130: the connection was the thing that got cut.
131: 
132: The failure this prevents: brevity that deletes the connective tissue and turns the
133: reply telegraphic, the reader rebuilds the argument the reply no longer states.
134: 
135: ---
136: 
137: ## 5. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT
138: 
139: - **Not a whole-reply rule.** Length, filler, tables and recovery live in
140:   [`communication.md`](communication.md), this rule stops where the reply as a whole begins.
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ## 6. SELF-CHECK
145: 
146: - [ ] Every sentence carries one idea, and no sentence stacks clauses a reader has to unpick.
147: - [ ] Every paragraph stands on its own, and the rhythm varies rather than marching.
148: - [ ] Replies use action words for arrows and symbols, say who does what, explain IDs,
149:   abbreviations and status codes, state what bare counts and labels mean, and turn
150:   fragments into full sentences.
151: - [ ] Each sentence says how it attaches to the one before, rather than sitting beside it.
152: - [ ] Where a sentence explains how something works, it names the moving part.
153: - [ ] Plain words, with exact names kept only for the things that have them.
154: - [ ] No em dash, no semicolon, no serial comma.
155: - [ ] Every path, hash, flag or ID in the reply is one the reader will act on, and no sentence carries more than two numbers.
156: - [ ] Nothing was compressed past the point where the reader has to re-expand it.

44: ---
45: 
46: ## 1. SENTENCES AND PARAGRAPHS
47: 
48: **One idea per sentence.** Short, declarative, subject-verb-object where that reads
49: naturally. When a sentence stacks clauses, split it.
50: 
51: **Atomic paragraphs.** Each chunk stands alone. A reader who lands mid-reply should be
52: able to act on the paragraph in front of them without reconstructing the four above it.
53: 
54: **Vary the rhythm** of sentence length and structure. Prefer prose when a list would
55: fragment a single argument.
56: 
57: The failure this prevents: a technically correct reply the reader has to parse twice.
58: 
59: **State the relation between sentences.** Each sentence opens by saying how it attaches
60: to the one before: because, but, therefore, for example.
61: 
62: The failure this prevents: juxtaposition fakes a logical link the writer never stated,
63: and the reader supplies their own, and supplies a different one.
64: 
65: **Name the mechanism.** When a sentence explains how something works, it names the
66: moving parts: what acts, what it acts on, what changes.
67: 
68: The failure this prevents: a model whose moving parts are never named, so the reader
69: can remember it and cannot check it.
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 2. WORDS
74: 
75: Plain words by default. Reserve exact names for the things that have them, languages,
76: frameworks, APIs, dependencies, commands.
77: 
78: Introduce unavoidable jargon one term at a time, in a sentence that defines it by use.
79: 
80: The failure this prevents: the reader stops reading and starts decoding, and stops
81: noticing whether they agree.
82: 
83: Do not ship replies in terse machine register. Replace arrows or symbols standing in for
84: verbs with action words. For stacked noun phrases, say who does what, using the
85: [HVR nominalization guidance](../skills/sk-doc/sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md#nominalization-and-stacked-compression).
86: Explain each ID, abbreviation or status code in plain words. Say what each bare count
87: or label measures and what it means. Turn sentence fragments into complete sentences
88: with a subject and verb, and join two of them with a full stop or a conjunction, never a
89: semicolon. The failure this prevents: readers have to guess at the action,
90: referent or result.
91: 
92: **Name an identifier only where the reader acts on it.** A path, hash, flag or ID earns its
93: place when the reader will run, open or check it. Elsewhere, say what the thing is in plain
94: words.
95: 
96: **One or two numbers to a sentence.** When the numbers are the point, give each its own
97: sentence or bullet.
98: 
99: The failure this prevents: a reply dense with names and figures the reader cannot use,
100: which buries the few they need.
101: 
102: ---
103: 
104: ## 3. PUNCTUATION THE READER TRIPS ON
105: 
106: **Never use an em dash.** Replace it with a comma, a full stop or a colon, whichever the
107: sentence actually wanted.
108: 
109: - **No semicolon.** Two sentences, or a conjunction.
110: - **No serial comma.** Drop it before the `and` or `or` that closes a list.
111: 
112: **The failure this prevents:** dashes read as authored voice to a human and as a tell to a
113: reader who has seen a lot of generated text.
114: 
115: The full standard is the Human Voice Rules, which `sk-doc` routes to. Load all of it when writing a document.
116: 
117: **In a reply, take its voice half and leave its document half.** The voice directives, the
118: vocabulary lists and the tell lists apply to anything a reader reads. The document-structure
119: sections do not. A message that presents the result of a long run is a reply by delivery and
120: a document by content, and it takes the voice half like any other reply.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 4. CONCISE IS NOT COMPRESSED
125: 
126: Concise cuts what the reader does not need and stops.
127: Compressed cuts further and takes the connective tissue with it: the because, the second
128: half of a contrast, the noun that a later "this" points back to. After a cut, check the
129: joints. If a sentence now opens on a "this" that the previous sentence no longer feeds,
130: the connection was the thing that got cut.
131: 
132: The failure this prevents: brevity that deletes the connective tissue and turns the
133: reply telegraphic, the reader rebuilds the argument the reply no longer states.
134: 
135: ---
136: 
137: ## 5. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT
138: 
139: - **Not a whole-reply rule.** Length, filler, tables and recovery live in
140:   [`communication.md`](communication.md), this rule stops where the reply as a whole begins.
141: 
142: ---
143: 
144: ## 6. SELF-CHECK
145: 
146: - [ ] Every sentence carries one idea, and no sentence stacks clauses a reader has to unpick.
147: - [ ] Every paragraph stands on its own, and the rhythm varies rather than marching.
148: - [ ] Replies use action words for arrows and symbols, say who does what, explain IDs,
149:   abbreviations and status codes, state what bare counts and labels mean, and turn
150:   fragments into full sentences.
151: - [ ] Each sentence says how it attaches to the one before, rather than sitting beside it.
152: - [ ] Where a sentence explains how something works, it names the moving part.
153: - [ ] Plain words, with exact names kept only for the things that have them.
154: - [ ] No em dash, no semicolon, no serial comma.
155: - [ ] Every path, hash, flag or ID in the reply is one the reader will act on, and no sentence carries more than two numbers.
156: - [ ] Nothing was compressed past the point where the reader has to re-expand it.
